item.title: Trump pushback, Biden 'disaster' and gender surprise: 5 key moments from Kansas Senate debate
item.description: Republican Sen. Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton clashed over Trump, transgender athletes and AI in a heated Kansas Senate debate on Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton sparred over President Donald Trump, immigration, Iran, transgender athletes, artificial intelligence and personal controversies during a contentious Kansas Senate debate Wednesday night.

The hourlong showdown came less than two weeks before Election Day as Marshall seeks a second term and Hamilton, a longtime pastor, tries to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932.

The race has drawn increased national attention as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the Senate, with Trump traveling to Kansas earlier this week to campaign for Marshall.

Here are five moments that stood out from Wednesday night's debate.

SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

The debate wasted little time getting contentious, opening with questions about controversies that have fueled attacks against both candidates.

Marshall was confronted with a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills.

"Every year we gave away $3 to $4 million of charity, but we also had a business," Marshall responded. "We had 300 employees, we had a mortgage payment, we had electric."

Hamilton, meanwhile, was questioned about his handling of allegations involving a volunteer at his church's summer camp who was accused of sexual abuse.

Hamilton acknowledged that he should have ensured the individual did not return to the camp following an initial investigation.

FROM 'THIRD REICH' TO âNOT THAT INFORMEDâ: SENATE DEBATES DELIVER FIREWORKS BEFORE MIDTERMS

"I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said. "That was a mistake on my part."

Trump became part of the debate after moderators played footage from the president's campaign appearance for Marshall in Kansas earlier in the week.

"And at this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot. Just pretend," Trump told the crowd.

Marshall was then asked whether Trump's support meant Kansans should expect him to back every part of the president's agenda.

"No," Marshall responded, saying there had been "multiple times" when he objected to Trump.

Pressed to identify a specific disagreement, Marshall pointed to recent immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and Trump's approach to beef imports.

"Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. My wife is always right," Marshall joked. "And President Trump is not always right."

Marshall nevertheless urged Trump voters to turn out for him, arguing that electing Hamilton could help Democrats capture the Senate.

The two rivals found themselves in agreement when the moderator asked each candidate how many genders there are.

"There's two. There's a boy and there's a girl," Marshall said. "I delivered 5,000 of them and almost half were boys and half were girls."

"There are two genders, male and female," Hamilton responded.

TOP TAKEAWAYS FROM JD VANCE TOWN HALL: COSTLY GAS, DC CORRUPTION, IMMIGRATION HOT TAKES AND THE WAR

The candidates then turned to the debate over transgender participation in women's sports.

Hamilton said decisions over athletic eligibility should generally be made locally but was unequivocal about whether biological males should compete against females.

"I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her," Hamilton said. "It's not a fair, fair fight."

Marshall argued that by high school, "boys need to be in boys sports, girls in girls sports," while accusing national Democrats of pushing "transgender ideology."

Hamilton later accused Marshall of using the issue to "pick on" and "bully" people.

Hamilton called for greater federal oversight of artificial intelligence and compared the emerging technology to the development of nuclear power and nuclear weapons.

"We developed a Nuclear Regulatory Commission. We need to do the same thing with AI," Hamilton said.

But when the moderator pressed him to identify specific federal regulations he would support, Hamilton acknowledged he did not yet have an answer.

"You know what? I'm not sure, to be honest," Hamilton said, arguing that even experts are struggling to understand the technology's potential dangers.

Marshall advocated a "light touch" approach focused on national security, transparency, protecting children and privacy, while slamming a one-size-fits-all global order for artificial intelligence advancement.

Hamilton pushed back sharply.

"This is an existential â potential existential threat to the human race," Hamilton said. "We can't just go with a light touch and hope everybody does their best."

BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH

Hamilton sought to put distance between himself and former President Joe Biden when moderators challenged the Democrat over his claim that he would "lead from the middle."

The moderator pointed to Hamilton's past donations to Democrats, including Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., before asking him to identify a progressive policy he opposed.

"The Biden policies when it came to the border were a disaster," Hamilton responded. "I believe in strong and secure borders."

"I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton added. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle."

Hamilton also reiterated during the debate that he would not support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for majority leader if Democrats capture control of the chamber.

item.title: 'Top Gun' star Tom Skerritt dead at 93
item.description: "Top Gun" star Tom Skerritt died of natural causes on Wednesday, his family confirmed to Fox News Digital. The actor, also known for his roles in "Picket Fences and "M*A*S*H," was 93.
item.content:encoded:
Tom Skerritt, best known for his roles in "Top Gun," "M*A*S*H," "Alien" and "Picket Fences" has died of natural causes. He was 93.  

"We are heartbroken by his loss," Skerritt's family said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives. He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world and helping others find and share their own voices."

They added, "We are incredibly grateful for the love and support being shown by his friends, colleagues, and fans. We ask for privacy as our family grieves. Information regarding a memorial will be shared at a later date."

This story is developing.

item.title: Chiefs place Josh Simmons on IR, raising questions about his entire future in the NFL
item.description: Josh Simmons' injured reserve placement raises deeper questions as conflicting timelines and pre-draft character concerns cloud the Chiefs' plans.
item.content:encoded:
The Kansas City Chiefs are placing left tackle Josh Simmons on injured reserve, the team announced. But the story runs deeper than a Super Bowl contender losing its starting left tackle for, most likely, the remainder of the season.

On Thursday, Chiefs Vice President of Sports Medicine and Performance Rich Burkholder told reporters that Simmons reported a leg issue on August 17, which the team determined was related to a bulging disc in his back. Burkholder said Simmons saw a specialist who recommended therapy instead of surgery.

Simmons has not played a down this season. He practiced in a limited capacity last week for the first time since reporting the injury to Burkholder. On Wednesday, the team listed him as a non-participant in practice for "back/non-injury personal reasons."

Burkholder said Simmons used the day to speak with his family before deciding it would be best to go on injured reserve. The designation requires Simmons to miss at least four games.

Put bluntly, skepticism about the Chiefs' version of events is warranted.

In August, reporters close to the team repeatedly reported that the injury was minor and that Simmons would return by Week 1. He didn't.

The next explanation was that the Chiefs had not placed him on injured reserve because they expected him to play within the first four weeks. He never did.

So what changed?

Burkholder says Simmons "plateaued" in his recovery. If so, head coach Andy Reid was unaware. On Monday, Reid said Simmons would continue to "ramp up" this week. On Wednesday morning, Reid did not include Simmons among the players who would not practice.

ONCE AGAIN, NO ONE KNOWS WHEN JOSH SIMMONS WILL RETURN — PERHAPS INCLUDING THE CHIEFS

The team's explanation is that Reid simply forgot to mention his starting left tackle's status.

Simmons' history adds another mysterious element to the situation. In fact, "mysterious" was the word ESPN NFL reporter Jeremy Fowler used to describe it last month.

Fowler's comment was notable because most other top national NFL reporters have avoided the story entirely. Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport host injury-related segments throughout the week on ESPN and NFL Network, yet neither has addressed the prolonged absence of Patrick Mahomes' starting left tackle. Meanwhile, they have provided countless updates on backup linebackers and kicker competitions.

"Mysterious" also describes Simmons' rookie season a year ago. He missed an entire month due to what the team called a "personal matter." ESPN reported at the time that members of the organization were unaware of why Simmons did not show up before a Week 6 matchup against the Detroit Lions.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

In August, Sports Illustrated's Matt Verderame added that Simmons left the team the night before the game and that there was a period during which the team did not know his whereabouts. OutKick had heard the same and emailed Chiefs general manager Brett Veach for comment. He did not respond.

There were also questions about Simmons ahead of the 2025 NFL Draft. Reports indicated that he had fully recovered from a patellar tendon injury but that some teams had taken him off their draft boards because of "character" concerns. Simmons fell to the final pick of the first round, where the Chiefs selected him 32nd overall.

The result: Simmons has played in just eight games over his first two NFL seasons.

Taken together, the lack of clarity surrounding his disappearance last season, the pre-draft reporting, and the conflicting expectations surrounding his current injury have naturally raised questions about his latest absence.

At the very least, it's fair to say Simmons has proven unreliable. Even the Chiefs appear unable to determine when, or if, he will play, as evidenced by their decision to wait more than two months after he initially reported the injury to place him on injured reserve.

At this point, no one can reasonably assume Simmons will return this season after he becomes eligible. Likewise, the Chiefs cannot go into another year with Simmons as their unquestioned starting left tackle.

Whether the issue is injuries, personal matters, character concerns, or some combination of the three, Simmons has proven that the Chiefs can't rely on him to fill one of the most important positions in football. His job is to protect Patrick Mahomes, the most valuable asset in the NFL.

No one should be surprised if Simmons never plays for the Chiefs again. Given the concerns that already existed before the draft, his future in the NFL is now legitimately in question.

item.title: Sports Illustrated adds Charley Hull to its swimsuit roster, NASCAR's nosedive & do we have anthem fatigue?
item.description: Charley Hull joins the SI Swimsuit 2027 roster as the LPGA star makes her debut, while Pat McAfee's Monday Night Football alt-broadcast stumbles.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news, and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

Over the hump and safely into another big week(end) of football. And baseball! Sure, Rays-Brewers ain't exactly Mets-Yankees from 2000, but the Fall Classic is still the Fall Classic.

Lord knows it's better than the whatever it is they're doing in the WNBA at the moment. Thank goodness that season is just about over. Goodness, it'll be nice when the curtains close on that league here in a few days.

It'll be smooth sailing after that! Just football, baseball, hockey and the NBA ... if you so choose. Beautiful time of year.

Let's roll.

Welcome to a Thursday Nightcaps — the one where LPGA star Charley Hull throws her bikini in the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit ring for the first time.

LPGA STAR CHARLEY HULL HAS FRIEND TO THANK FOR NOT GETTING DRUNKEN FOREHEAD TATTOO AFTER NIGHT OUT AT THE CLUB

That's right. We've got a new rookie on this year's roster, and she's a modern-day Andrew Luck in terms of hype. What a steal for SI. Well done.

What else? I've got Pat McAfee's first ESPN alt-cast of a Monday night game going terribly, the big-wigs over at NASCAR HQ experiencing a similar situation, and we've got more national anthem drama ... somehow.

The president has even weighed in this time! I'll be honest with you, I have national anthem drama fatigue. I'm just over it. I don't care anymore.

Beyond the obvious disgust, do you guys care anymore? I'm curious.

OK, grab you your favorite horror movie in anticipation of tomorrow's National Horror Movie Day, and settle in for a Thursday 'Cap!

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Those of you who have been in this class since the beginning (nearly five years now!) know that I'm a horror movie buff. I love that stuff. I grew up watching scary movies with my mom.

In fact, she accidentally took me to a screening of Rob Zombie's Halloween II as a teenager, and the whole movie basically just turned out to be a bunch of sex scenes. We didn't talk for two days.

Anyway, I maintain that Halloween is the greatest horror movie of all time. It's certainly the best slasher movie out there. The theme song. The suspense. The ridiculous sequels and spin-offs. It's just perfect. The entire franchise is great, except the most recent movie, which was trash.

Mount Rushmore of Halloween movies? Sure, why not?!

Honorable mentions: Halloween 6 (Paul Rudd's debut!) and the first Halloween of the most recent reboot trilogy. The other two STUNK.

LPGA STAR CHARLEY HULL DITCHES THE LINKS FOR A BIKINI GIRLS TRIP, DOLPHINS-BENGALS FAN FIGHT & 'BAMA NO-CALL!

And that concludes the cinema portion of today's class. You're welcome!

OK, let's get this thing started with someone who is the opposite of scary: LPGA star, Charley Hull!

Turns out, our girl is dipping her toe into the SI Swimsuit waters:

From Sports Illustrated:

Professional golfer Charley Hull will make her SI Swimsuit debut in the 2027 issue. After turning pro in 2013, Hull quickly became the youngest player to ever represent Europe in the Solheim Cup at the age of 17. Now 30, the English golfer is a three-time LPGA Tour winner who reached her career high of No. 3 in the Rolex Women’s World Golf Rankings in February 2026.

Welcome to the show, Charley Hull! OutKick has been following Hull since the beginning, so it's good to see her getting the credit she deserves.

She may be European, but make no mistake about it ... she's a patriot.

Check out what she said to Joe Kinsey last month about Sydney Sweeney's gambling ad that sent the left into a death spiral:

"The amount of backlash that (it) is getting, I just don't understand the way people's brains work. They're making a big deal out of nothing. It's an actress slash model modeling for an advert. And I think she owns the company as well."

Yep. I think she'll do just fine in her new endeavor.

Worse comes to worst, she'll certainly do better than Pat McAfee's alt-broadcast of Monday Night Football earlier this week:

So, here's the thing ...

A lot of folks say those embarrassing ratings are a sign that fans have "Pat McAfee fatigue." I disagree.

I think we have "alt-broadcast fatigue." WHY do we need multiple broadcasts of a game? I don't get it. You go to watch a college football game on ESPN nowadays, and you accidentally end up watching the "Skycast" view, which is just an announcer-less view of the game from a camera above the action. That's it.

WHY do we need that?!

Why do we need an "alt-cast"? Just give us the stupid game on the stupid channel and leave us alone. We don't need to hear what another group of analysts thinks of the game. We don't need to watch the game from their sideline perspective. We don't need a "Next-Gen" broadcast of all the stats nobody cares about.

Just let us watch the game! It ain't McAfee fatigue. It's streaming fatigue. That's it.

Don't believe me? Ask NASCAR!

Look at that number! Do you understand how bad that is? Sunday's NASCAR playoff race at Phoenix drew just 1.2 million viewers. That's unfathomably bad.

I wrote about it this morning and really got into the weeds. I won't do that here because we all have better things to do, but feel free to dive in.

Bottom line? NASCAR's top series has been on network TV all of seven times this year. Seven. That means the other 26 races have been on either cable, or streaming. That ain't gonna work.

Again, folks are tired of the extra nonsense. We've gone too far with streaming and alt-broadcasts. Simpler is better. NASCAR is now learning that the hard way.

Finally, on the way out, let's check in on the latest national anthem scandal on the hardwood:

I'd like to leave the class with a question today ...

Are y'all over the anthem stuff? I don't mean that in a bad way. I'm not saying it's not ridiculous behavior, because it is.

But do we really care how LeBron James acts before games? Is it really worth getting upset over LEBRON JAMES in 2026? Or at the insufferable WNBA girls? We know who they are. We know what they believe, and how they act.

Why do we care anymore? They're all gaslighters. They're all virtue-signalers. They're all insufferable.

At this point, I'd prefer just treat them as such and ignore the nonsense.

How do you feel? Let me know!

See you tomorrow.

Zach.Dean@OutKick.com

item.content:encoded:
A senior on the Utah football team has been suspended after he was accused of rape.

Jamal Wallace, a defensive lineman, is currently under investigation amid the allegation – he also is accused of sharing videos of the incident on social media.

Wallace was arrested earlier this month on charges that include five misdemeanors.

item.title: Supreme Court Justice Kagan warns some conservative rulings have been 'destructive of our democracy'
item.description: Justice Elena Kagan warned that Supreme Court rulings on gerrymandering and campaign finance have created a democracy that "doesn't work" for everyone.
item.content:encoded:
Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan suggested Tuesday that some recent decisions by her conservative colleagues have undermined democracy, while admitting at times they had also pushed back against the Trump administration.

Kagan took part in a discussion on recent U.S. Supreme Court decisions while speaking at Catholic University's Columbus School of Law. She specifically took issue with cases like Louisiana v. Callais, which ruled in a 6-3 decision that race-based gerrymandering of congressional districts was unconstitutional.

In her dissent, Kagan called the decision the "latest chapter in the majority's now-completed demolition of the Voting Rights Act" and she continued to criticize election and campaign finance decisions made by the court.

KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS

"Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions," Kagan said, according to NBC News.

She went on to warn that decisions that undermined voters' ability to choose their candidates were "very destructive of our democracy."

"I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn't work as well as it should," Kagan said.

SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PINPOINTS WHAT AMERICANS MISUNDERSTAND ABOUT HIM AND HIS COLLEAGUES

She also criticized the conservative view of originalism in the Supreme Court, calling it "misconceived" and "not a very good match with the Constitution we have."

Kagan claimed that these and other decisions have contributed to the country becoming more "polarized," particularly around campaign finance.

"I think you know the people of America look around this political system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they're right," she said.

CONSERVATIVE GROUPS SAY JUSTICE KAGAN CANNOT BE IMPARTIAL IN UPCOMING SUPREME COURT CLIMATE LITIGATION

However, Kagan stopped short of accusing the court of being beholden to President Donald Trump, pointing out several cases where even conservative justices "definitely pushed back" on his agenda. Trump nominated three of the current justices on the court in Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett.

In a comment to Fox News Digital, Heritage Foundation Senior Legal Fellow of Courts and the Constitution Zack Smith denounced Kagan and what he characterized as far-left politicians' efforts to delegitimize SCOTUS decisions.

"The job of the Court is not to play politics with its decisions. Instead, its job is to faithfully apply the Constitution and other laws as they are written. Justice Kagan has disagreed with the majority of her colleagues in some of those decisions, but that doesn't mean they are illegitimate or even wrongly decided," Smith said.

item.title: RILEY GAINES: Call Her Daddy's advice is a dangerous recipe for lifelong regret
item.description: Alex Cooper and Sophia Bush's viral marriage advice sparks a deeper debate about feminism, sacrifice, and what empowerment truly means for women.
item.content:encoded:
In a viral exchange this week, Call Her Daddy host Alex Cooper and actress Sophia Bush offered young women a familiar piece of relationship advice: If you're questioning whether to leave your marriage because you fear you won't find someone better, the answer is always yes.

Bush went further, suggesting that the fear of being too old or unreasonable for wanting more is a product of the patriarchy.

Cooper built her brand largely by celebrating sexual experimentation, including encouraging young women to engage in highly explicit sexual experimentation early in dating. This is the same podcast Kamala Harris joined prior to the 2024 election, but I digress.

RILEY GAINES FIRES BACK AT ALEX COOPER’S GRAPHIC DATING ADVICE: ‘IT IS NOT EMPOWERMENT. IT IS POISON’

Bush is now on her third marriage, with the first one lasting 5 months, the second lasting about a year, and the third to a woman.

These are the voices our culture elevates as influential guides for young women. But enough about the who. Let's examine the what.

The exchange reveals a worldview in which something better is always waiting. That personal and fleeting dissatisfaction is sufficient reason to abandon a commitment, and that the pursuit of more is interchangeable with empowerment.

More what, exactly?

More excitement? More affirmation? More freedom? Another relationship that will inevitably encounter the same imperfections as the last?

At what point do we consider whether the relentless pursuit of more is precisely what leaves us feeling we have less?

AMERICAN WOMEN HAVE BEEN LIED TO ABOUT MOTHERHOOD AND IT’S TIME TO FIX IT

For decades, women have been sold a particular vision of liberation. Prioritize your career. Maximize your independence. Explore your sexuality without consequence. Reject marriage, delay motherhood, and never compromise your ambitions for someone else's needs. Above all, put yourself first.

We were assured that freedom from traditional obligations would produce unprecedented happiness.

TRADITIONAL TWO-PARENT FAMILIES VANISH FROM BIG AMERICAN CITIES AS 'MARRIAGE DESERTS' EXPAND

If that were true, we would certainly see it in society. But instead, what was promised as empowerment has delivered emptiness.

Despite constant technological connectivity, loneliness and social isolation remain pervasive. Anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation are serious concerns, particularly among younger generations. These problems have many causes, and attributing them all to feminism would be intellectually dishonest. But ignoring the possibility that our prevailing philosophy has failed to deliver its promised fulfillment would be equally foolish.

We’ve spent decades dismantling the institutions that tether individuals to one another, only to discover that autonomy is a poor substitute for belonging.

Perhaps most tragically, we’ve taught women to regard sacrifice as oppression rather than an indispensable part of love.

Consider the contradiction.

A woman who sacrifices her time, energy, and health to climb the corporate ladder is celebrated as ambitious. A woman making comparable sacrifices for her husband and children is too often regarded as having surrendered her potential to the patriarchy. Why?

ONE GROUP OF MARRIED AMERICANS IS HAVING MORE SEX — AND HAPPIER MARRIAGES

I am profoundly grateful for the opportunities women have today. I’ve competed as a collegiate athlete, traveled the country, built a career, and achieved things my younger self could never have imagined. But no professional accolade, public recognition, or personal achievement has given me the satisfaction and purpose I’ve found in marriage and motherhood.

They require more of me than anything I've ever done (even a 200-yard butterfly). It's hard. But "hard" and "bad" are not synonymous.

Motherhood fundamentally changed my understanding of success. There's something remarkably clarifying about being needed by someone who has nothing to offer you in return except themselves.

I don't view it as a limitation on my freedom, but instead a revelation of what my freedom is for.

Which brings me back to Cooper, who just welcomed her first child with her husband.

I genuinely congratulate her. But there's irony in continuing to promote perpetual self-prioritization through meaningless hookups and "girl-bossing" while building a life rooted in the very institutions modern feminism so often characterizes as oppressive.

Perhaps motherhood will offer her the same perspective it offered me: that the deepest fulfillment isn't found in putting yourself first, but in loving someone enough to put them first.

Of course, marriage and motherhood aren't the only paths to meaning. Women who are single, childless, or unable to have children are no less valuable. Purpose takes countless forms, but lasting meaning generally requires looking beyond ourselves.

This is hardly a novel insight. Christianity has taught for centuries that a life centered exclusively on the self is ultimately impoverished. Love is not merely a feeling to be pursued while convenient. It is a commitment expressed through action, fidelity, humility, and sacrifice.

Our culture treats these virtues as antiquated burdens, then wonders why so many feel unmoored.

Cooper and Bush's advice is troubling because it reduces marriage to personal optimization. Marriage becomes less a covenant to honor than an arrangement to continually reassess against hypothetical alternatives.

There are legitimate reasons marriages end, including abuse and betrayal. But reflexively encouraging people to search for something better without acknowledging the responsibilities of commitment isn't teaching empowerment like the self-proclaimed feminists like to claim. It teaches disposability.

A generation encouraged to keep every option open may eventually discover that life's most meaningful commitments require closing certain doors.

Choosing a spouse. Raising children. Building a family. Practicing faith. Serving a community. Creating something that will endure long after your own ambitions have faded.

Like everything associated with risk, these commitments impose limits, but I’ve found they also give life its depth.

Women deserve more than the hollow assurance that happiness is perpetually waiting in the next relationship, promotion, or reinvention of themselves. They deserve to know that fulfillment isn't always found in acquiring more and finding someone that validates your every desire. Often, it's found in giving more.

The great lie of modern empowerment isn't that women are capable of extraordinary things. It's that a life devoted primarily to ourselves is the most extraordinary thing we can aspire to.

We should stop telling women that the ultimate goal is to have everything and start reminding them of the beauty of having something worth giving everything for.

And perhaps the grass isn't always greener on the other side.

It’s greener where you water it.

item.title: Supreme Court justice turns on her own court with dire warning about American democracy
item.description: Elena Kagan argued the Supreme Court's gerrymandering and campaign finance rulings are destabilizing democracy and driving political polarization.
item.content:encoded:
Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan made the case that recent rulings from the conservative-majority high court are destabilizing democracy, suggesting that it isn't working "as well as it should."

The remarks from the liberal justice came during a closed discussion before faculty and students at Catholic University's law school in Washington, D.C.

The discussion between Kagan and law professor Joel Alicea Alicia, who previously clerked for Justice Samuel Alito, comes just weeks after the Supreme Court began its new term, during which it's expected to rule in major cases that will determine the scope of gun rights and state election integrity laws, among other issues.

The conversation also comes less than two weeks before the midterm elections as President Donald Trump and Republican state lawmakers have pushed for new congressional maps drawn to favor Republicans and bolster their chances of maintaining control of the House. Democratic-led states have responded by redrawing their own maps, fueling ongoing lawsuits and court battles.

SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE

Kagan pointed to the Supreme Court’s 2019 ruling in Rucho v. Common Cause, in which she dissented, as the beginning of a "race to the bottom." She argued that the decision, which barred federal courts from invalidating maps solely because they unfairly favor one political party, deprived "masses of citizens" of their "rights to voting equality."

Kagan suggested that the influx of gerrymandered maps is "driving people away from the center toward the wings, toward the extremes.

"Making what I think is, unfortunately, a too polarized country even more so," Kagan said.

Kagan also criticized rulings from the previous term, including the court’s decision limiting campaign finance restrictions and its ruling that made it more difficult to draw majority-minority congressional districts under the Voting Rights Act.

"Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions," Kagan said.

"I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t work as well as it should."

DESANTIS SIGNS FLORIDA REDISTRICTING MAP TO POTENTIALLY FLIP 4 HOUSE SEATS RED

Last term, the Supreme Court struck down federal limits on how much state and national political parties could spend in coordination with their candidates.

Meanwhile, Kagan argued in dissent that the limits were necessary to prevent wealthy donors from working around direct contribution caps and that striking them down effectively allowed a political party to become an "alternative checking account" for a candidate.

"The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare," Kagan said. "And they’re right."

Kagan, who was appointed to the court by President Barack Obama in 2010, argued that it was in a much better position when there was greater ideological balance.

"There was a period of time where the court was in a better place, and the country was in a better place because the court was more balanced, and it was unclear whether the court could push through anybody’s program."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"Nobody in America thought that the court was in the pocket of any one group or any one party," she said. "And the court had a kind of legitimacy. When the court has a legitimacy of that kind, it helps to create a stable country."

However, Kagan pushed back against the characterization that the conservative-leaning court simply rubber-stamped Trump's entire agenda. She pointed to previous rulings by the high court rejecting birthright citizenship restrictions, tariffs and Trump's restrictions on mail-in voting.

"It’s why the president sometimes really has not very nice things to say about the court’s decisions and some of my colleagues," Kagan said.

item.title: Ilhan Omar says she lives 'paycheck to paycheck' as DOJ probes financial disclosures
item.description: Ilhan Omar claims she lives "paycheck to paycheck," despite earning $174,000 and facing scrutiny over financial disclosures tied to Tim Mynett.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., described herself as a member of the "working class" who lives "paycheck to paycheck" during an interview with MS NOW host Chris Hayes on Wednesday night.

"I mean, it’s, you know, working — working class, I guess, like paycheck to paycheck still," Omar said. "We’ve got four kids, and we live, I think, like a basic life. I have a Toyota Camry that’s from 2016."

Omar's characterization of her finances comes despite her $174,000 annual congressional salary and scrutiny over financial disclosures that once listed assets tied to her husband as being worth as much as $30 million.

The comments came during Omar’s first public appearance since Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents searched her Washington, D.C., residence on Oct. 12 as part of an investigation into possible immigration-related offenses.

ILHAN OMAR BELIEVES TRUMP RAID ON HOME WAS MEANT TO 'INTIMIDATE AND SCARE PEOPLE' FROM VOTING

Since the raid, the representative has used the investigation twice as a reason to publicly fundraise.

"That goes a long way as we fight Trump and his administration for trying to intimidate me and so many people right before the midterm elections," Omar said in a video she uploaded to social media on Wednesday. "We know that they’re running scared. We’re not going to be intimidated. We’re not going to be silenced."

The Democratic National Committee has also sent out its own fundraising email based on Omar’s campaign request for money.

"It’s Ilhan Omar — Trump’s DHS agents just carried out a raid and search of my home," the email says. "This is a drastic escalation of the ludicrous, partisan investigation that they launched into my immigration status."

ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME

Omar also acknowledged during the MS NOW interview that the federal agents who searched her home were "polite" and left the property in good condition, even folding some of her clothes.

"When they left, what did you do?" Hayes asked Omar.

"I just went back around the house just trying to make sure everything was put back," Omar replied. "And they did a really good job in putting everything back in its place. They actually even folded some of my clothing that [was] not folded. So it was … a very bizarre [situation]."

The Minnesota Democrat added that she thought the HSI agents who raided her home were "intrusive, but polite."

"And yeah, they, they left the house, I think, you know, in good shape," she told MS NOW.

Omar claimed during the interview that the federal agents were searching her house for four to five hours. She added that they left the raid with more than a dozen items, including notebooks and a children’s Somali-language phrasebook.

"[That] was why I was surprised when they handed me the receipt for the items that they take in, to do that long of a search and to walk away with 17 items, of like 10 that were just notebooks and, like, old phones. Was such a bizarre, bizarre thing," Omar said.

A separate Justice Department investigation is examining Omar’s financial disclosures, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said during an appearance on Fox News’ "America Reports."

The disclosures previously showed that the reported value of two businesses tied to Omar’s husband, Tim Mynett, rose from as much as $51,000 in 2023 to as much as $30 million in 2024, according to House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky.

Omar later amended the filing, saying the original figures were the result of an accounting error. The amended disclosure listed the couple’s assets at between $18,004 and $95,000. Omar has denied wrongdoing, and no criminal charges have been filed against her in connection with the disclosures.

Mynett’s businesses include eStCru, a winery, and Rose Lake Capital, an investment firm. The winery has reportedly shut down.

ILHAN OMAR RAID SPARKS OMINOUS PREDICTION FROM WATCHDOG: 'THEY PROBABLY GOT THE GOODS'

On Fox News’ "Sunday Night in America," Comer told host Trey Gowdy that his committee’s initial review of Omar’s disclosures identified multiple issues that could justify further investigative steps.

"First of all, not only was there a huge discrepancy in the financial disclosure form, there was the winery that was the big base of her $25 million listing on her financial disclosure form," Comer said. "That winery has, according to the press, been shut down because of fraud."

In a February letter to Mynett, Comer noted that Omar’s 2023 disclosure listed her stake in eStCru as being worth between $15,001 and $50,000.

"The following year, her financial disclosure form listed a stake in eStCru ‘worth between $1,000,001 and $5,000,000,’" Comer wrote. "There are serious public concerns about how your businesses increased so dramatically in value only a year after reporting very limited assets."

A rank-and-file House member’s annual salary is $174,000. Members may also participate in the federal Thrift Savings Plan and qualify for a pension under the Federal Employees Retirement System, though eligibility and benefit amounts depend on factors including age, years of service and salary history.

The financial investigation remains ongoing.

item.title: Jack Osbourne says doctors warned Ozzy not to perform final concert just 17 days before his death
item.description: Jack Osbourne reveals doctors warned Ozzy Osbourne about his heart and artery issues before the Birmingham farewell concert, but he refused to stop.
item.content:encoded:
Jack Osbourne is reflecting on the weeks leading up to his father Ozzy Osbourne's death, revealing the stark warning doctors gave the rock legend before his final performance.

During an appearance on "Great Company with Jamie Laing," Jack recalled how doctors urged the Black Sabbath frontman not to take the stage at his farewell concert due to serious health concerns.

"They basically were just saying like you've got so many things going on," Jack explained. "We recommend you don't do this because the energy expenditure."

.OZZY OSBOURNE KNEW THE END WAS NEAR DURING FINAL PERFORMANCE, FRIEND SAYS 

Jack revealed that his father had been dealing with multiple medical complications leading up to the show.

"There was like something with his heart and he had some like artery stuff going on," he said, adding that Ozzy had experienced "a ton of medical kind of mishaps leading up to the show."

Despite the warnings, the Prince of Darkness was determined to give fans one final performance.

OZZY OSBOURNE'S SON JACK SHARES PRIVATE FAMILY MOMENTS IN EMOTIONAL TRIBUTE TO LATE FATHER 

"They were just like energetically, this is going to ... this is not good. This is not good. Like you don't have it in you," Jack recalled of the doctors' concerns.

His father's response was simple: "I'm doing it."

Just 17 days later, Ozzy died at the age of 76.

KELLY OSBOURNE SAYS SHE 'WASN'T WELL' WHILE FACING HARSH SCRUTINY, BODY-SHAMING AFTER DAD OZZY'S DEATH

Although Jack admitted he was heartbroken over his father's death, he said he wasn't angry about the rock legend's decision to perform despite the medical warnings.

"But he wanted his journey. And so I can't ... I'm not angry at that," Jack explained.

"I think everyone wants to at least have some say in how they go," he continued. "Obviously, deeply heartbroken that he's gone but also he went the way he wanted to."

Ozzy performed his final show with his Black Sabbath bandmates Geezer Butler, Tony Iommi and Bill Ward at his "Back to the Beginning" farewell concert in Birmingham, England, on July 5, 2025.

KELLY OSBOURNE BLASTS DEE SNIDER AS 'SPECTACULARLY CLASSLESS' FOR CLAIMING OZZY DIDN’T WRITE HIS OWN SONGS

The 10-hour show, hosted by Jason Momoa, featured performances from Metallica, Guns N' Roses, Jack Black, Steven Tyler and more.

For the closing set, according to a photo posted on X and various videos, the legendary rocker was lifted onto the stage while seated on a black throne adorned with skulls and topped with a black bat. He performed hits including "Crazy Train" and "Mama I'm Coming Home" while remaining seated throughout the set.

ROD STEWART TURNS TO OXYGEN TANK MID-CONCERT AFTER NEARLY COLLAPSING ONSTAGE

"It's so good to be on this stage... You have no idea how I feel," Ozzy told the crowd, according to Planet Rock Radio. "Thank you from the bottom of my heart."

The Black Sabbath frontman died on July 22, 2025. He was 76.

OZZY AND SHARON OSBOURNE'S LONGTIME LOS ANGELES HOME HITS THE MARKET FOR $17M AFTER HIS DEATH AT 76

"It is with more sadness than mere words can convey that we have to report that our beloved Ozzy Osbourne has passed away this morning," his family said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital at the time. "He was with his family and surrounded by love. We ask everyone to respect our family privacy at this time."

Ozzy's death certificate listed cardiac arrest, acute myocardial infarction, coronary artery disease and Parkinson's disease.

Jack's emotional reflections come as his mother, Sharon Osbourne, has also opened up about the final moments she shared with her husband of 43 years.

During an appearance on "Piers Morgan Uncensored," Sharon, 73, broke down in tears as she recalled her last conversation with the rock legend.

Sharon explained that Ozzy had been "up and down" throughout the night before waking her around 4:30 a.m.

"He said, 'Wake up' and [I said] 'I'm already bloody awake, you've woken me up,'" Sharon remembered. "And he said, 'Kiss me.' And then he said, 'Hug me tight.'"

Sharon emotionally confirmed that those were the last words her husband said to her before he died later that morning.

The former "The Talk" host explained that Ozzy would often wake up early to exercise and had followed his usual routine on the day of his death.

"He went downstairs and worked out for 20 minutes and passed away," she said.

Sharon recalled hearing "screaming" inside their home before rushing downstairs and discovering that attempts were being made to revive her husband.

"They were trying to resuscitate him and I'm like 'Don't. Leave him. Leave him. You can't. He's gone.' I knew instantly he's gone," she recalled.

"And they tried and tried and then they took him by helicopter to the hospital and they tried and it's like, 'He's gone. Just leave him.'"

Sharon admitted that her grief following Ozzy's death was so overwhelming that she "couldn't function." She also struggled with regrets about their final exchange.

"If only I'd have told him I loved him more. If only I'd have held him tighter," she said through tears.

Fox News Digital's Ashley Hume and Tracy Wright contributed to this post.

item.title: Team USA star Brady Tkachuk endures 'you eat crayons' taunt in wild return to Canada
item.description: Brady Tkachuk's return to Ottawa was pure chaos as Senators fans unleashed creative chants, jersey tosses, and boos during his Panthers visit.
item.content:encoded:
Ever since Brady Tkachuk asked the Ottawa Senators for a trade and they shipped him to the division rival Florida Panthers, everyone has had Tuesday night's game in the Canadian capital marked on their "Far Side" desk calendars.

At least I did, and boy, was it wild.

Tkachuk had been the franchise centerpiece in Ottawa, but things started to change after he and the U.S. men's hockey team won Olympic gold over Canada at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan.

Remember that? Remember when the U.S. beat Canada for Olympic gold? It was great.

Anyway, that led to repeated questions about his commitment to the franchise. By the summer, that commitment was no more as he asked for a ticket out and landed in South Florida with his brother, Matthew.

OTTAWA SENATORS OWNER CLAIMS KEITH TKACHUK AND MATTHEW TKACHUK SWAYED BRADY'S TRADE REQUEST

Now, Sens fans were understandably perturbed by this as the club is without a doubt on the rise, and boy, did they make their displeasure known.

I mean, if there are supercuts of the various chants a crowd hurls at a former player, then I think it's safe to say that the current relationship is frosty at best.

I've got to hand it to them; they were creative. I never thought I'd hear an NHL arena chanting "You eat crayons," but I just did.

But Tkachuk, who has been on a heater lately that included back-to-back natural hat tricks, didn't let those chants get under his skin. For starters, he scored the opening goal of the game.

TEAM USA HOCKEY BROTHERS CONNECT TO PULL OFF HISTORIC NHL FEAT IN DOMINANT PERFORMANCE

The only downside was that the Senators scored the next five to win 5-1.

But there were more hilarious moments, the biggest being Tkachuk's full-on heel turn when the team showed a tribute video that got mercilessly booed by the crowd.

While most NHLers would try to downplay it with a quick, subtle wave or nod, Tkachuk did a full victory lap like he was returning after 1,400 games in the league.

That's an all-timer. Even the angriest Senators fan had to be like, "Alright, that was pretty funny."

Tkachuk also got into it with his former teammates like Ridley Greig.

Then, as if all of that wasn't enough, Sens fans started raining down their old Tkachuk jerseys.

What a scene. You don't see too many returns go down like that. But if Tkachuk was rattled by it, he sure didn't let it show during his postgame interview.

You've got to think that Tkachuk is going to hear something like this any time he steps on the Canadian Tire Centre ice for the rest of his career. Also, probably best to steer clear of any Ottawa area restaurants.

Y'know, play it safe.

item.title: Ilhan Omar is not the Minnesota congresswoman’s 'real name': sources
item.description: Federal investigators say the congresswoman's real name is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, as U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro moves to keep the warrant sealed.
item.content:encoded:
Ilhan Omar is not the "real name" of the Minnesota congresswoman, Fox News Digital has learned.

Her real name is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, according to two people familiar with the ongoing investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman, including a law enforcement source.

And if proven in court that Omar has lived her "entire life under an alias," a former Minnesota federal immigration judge tells Fox News Digital that every single form she ever filled out could be "called into question."

On Wednesday, U.S. District Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro filed a motion seeking to prevent the federal search warrant for the congresswoman’s home from being unsealed, which was requested by several media outlets. The motion says the federal government is not yet finished executing the search warrant, and that it shouldn’t be unsealed yet.

"Before the Court are three Applications to unseal ex parte materials and proceedings related to a federal search warrant for the personal residence in the District of Columbia of Congresswoman Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar…" the motion begins.

"That's not her real name," one source said when asked why the motion used the "a/k/a Ilhan Adbullahi Omar" language.

Fox News Digital first reported in the midst of the search of the lawmaker's Washington, D.C. residence that federal investigators are probing whether she or her father committed fraud when filling out her immigration paperwork.

Investigators obtained the elected official’s DNA and seized her personal phone and passport during the Oct. 12 pre-dawn raid.

FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE

Omar’s sister, Sahra Noor, was questioned by federal investigators last week in relation to the probe, Fox News Digital exclusively reported.

Conservative personality Will Chamberlain first posted the motion on X speculating that the "DOJ believes [Omar] is present in the United States under a false identity."

Fox News Digital has now learned from multiple sources familiar with the investigation that Omar is not the congresswoman’s birth name.

REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES

Omar has publicly confirmed that she does not have a birth certificate.

In an official U.S. House biography, her birthday is listed as Oct. 14, 1982, and states that she was born in Mogadishu, Somalia. She says she came to the U.S. with her family as refugees fleeing war-torn Somalia in 1995, when she was a minor.

Omar has not been charged with a crime, and materials presented by prosecutors are only allegations.

Attorneys for the embattled congresswoman did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Nathan Hansen, a former federal immigration judge from Minnesota, listed the extent to which the supposed name change could impact the case against the congresswoman.

"You think of all the types of documents somebody like her might have filled out," he said. "There'd be federal student loan and student aid applications, maybe federal housing related applications, maybe public assistance applications, passport applications, passport information and driver's license information, Real I.D. information [and] voting information."

ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS

He said if someone has lived their entire lives under an alias, there are many criminal charges that could be levied.

"Sometimes they might say that that would be a wire fraud charge, they always add that one," said Hansen. "And that's pretty broad. But, you know, a lot of these documents are sworn under penalty of perjury."

"If this is not, like, a real legal name, it's got some legal backing to it that every type of government form she's filled out in her entire existence might be called into question," Hansen said.

ILHAN OMAR SHOULD BE JAILED, DEPORTED IF CITIZENSHIP FRAUD PROVEN, TOP HOUSE REPUBLICAN SAYS

The representative for Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District in the U.S. House, has long faced allegations that she married her brother for immigration purposes.

In 2009, she legally married a man named Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. The pair split in 2017. The following year, she was elected to Congress. In 2020, she married her third husband, political consultant Tim Mynett.

In Omar's first public interview since the raid on her home, she sat down with MS NOW’s Chris Hayes. During that interview, she once again denied those allegations, calling them "insane."

ILHAN OMAR BELIEVES TRUMP RAID ON HOME WAS MEANT TO 'INTIMIDATE AND SCARE PEOPLE' FROM VOTING

"You’re not related to him at all?" Hayes asked. "There’s not some weird kernel of truth…?"

"Not to my knowledge," she replied.

In the wake of the raid, Omar has accused President Donald Trump and his administration of targeting her politically.

"This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," she said in a statement on X.

HOMAN SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD BE STRIPPED OF NATURALIZATION, DEPORTED IF IMMIGRATION FRAUD IS PROVEN

"For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," the post continued. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."

Fox News Digital reached out to a spokesperson for Omar, but did not hear back at time of publication.

item.title: Australia pastor case 'canary in the coal mine' for American Christian freedoms: TPUSA leader
item.description: Lucas Miles of Turning Point USA says he contacted the White House Faith Office urging Trump to pressure Australia over a church investigation.
item.content:encoded:
A Turning Point USA faith leader is calling on President Donald Trump to intervene after Australian lawmakers grilled a Christian church leader about his religious beliefs, including whether he influences members' marriages, hairstyles and even pet ownership.

Lucas Miles, vice president of faith at Turning Point USA, told Fox News Digital he contacted the White House Faith Office and several administration officials over what he described as a politically motivated investigation into the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church.

"We've reached out to the faith office, we've reached out to several members of the administration to make sure that they're aware of this," Miles said. "We're hoping to see some response and action soon."

UK LAWMAKER WARNS IT’S ‘OPEN SEASON’ ON CHRISTIANS AS HE SOUNDS ALARM OVER ‘TWO-TIER JUSTICE’

The controversy intensified during an Oct. 16 parliamentary hearing examining allegations of coordinated political activity by church members during Australia's 2025 federal election.

Independent MP Monique Ryan questioned the church's global leader, Bruce Hales, about whether members considered him an "elect vessel" or a direct messenger from God. She also asked whether members sought his guidance on marriage, housing, pets, clothing and facial hair.

Liberal MP Ben Small objected to the questioning, calling it "patently ridiculous" and "so far off the terms of reference for this inquiry."

Another lawmaker interjected that hairstyles had no bearing on electoral matters, while the committee chair allowed the questioning to continue.

"When an Australian parliamentary committee tasked with investigating election matters begins interrogating a Christian leader about his theological convictions, serious questions must be asked about the purpose of the inquiry," Miles said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

"Bruce Hales was summoned to answer questions about electoral conduct, not to defend the doctrines of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church before the government," he added.

BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: THE WAR ON CHRISTIANS IS REAL AND THE WORLD CAN NO LONGER STAY SILENT

Miles argued that the line of questioning may illustrate a broader threat to religious freedom.

"The troubling shift from election oversight to religious scrutiny gives every appearance of a politically motivated witch hunt," he said.

Hales denied directing, funding or coordinating political campaigning during the 2025 election, maintaining that church members acted independently.

"I had no involvement whatsoever in relation to any members who volunteered or took part in any aspect of the 2025 federal election," Hales told the committee.

Lawmakers questioned whether a sermon in which Hales said Australia needed to be "happy again, smiling again" influenced members' political activities, citing subsequent campaign messaging that echoed his words.

His son, Gareth, acknowledged encouraging people already involved in campaigning but denied directing an organized church campaign.

CHRISTIAN WOMAN PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO NEW 'ORWELLIAN' CHARGES FOR STANDING AND SILENT PRAYER

The committee is also examining allegations of intimidation and coordinated campaigning during the election. Church leaders have denied organizing or condoning improper conduct.

Hales said he did not support harassment or intimidation and maintained that individual members should be accountable for their own actions.

"In a free society, government has every right to investigate violations of election law, but it has no business putting Christian doctrine on trial," Miles said.

The Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, which traces its roots back roughly 200 years, says its roughly 55,000 members worldwide follow a "Doctrine of Separation," distancing themselves from certain secular activities and practices they believe conflict with biblical teachings.

The church rejects descriptions of the denomination as a cult, maintaining that its members freely practice their faith and contribute to their communities through businesses and charitable initiatives.

The hearing also turned to the United States when Sen. Steph Hodgins-May questioned Hales about Turning Point USA's support for the church and whether church leaders had met with the Trump administration.

Hales said he had never met Trump but understood that some church members in New York had briefly met the president.

Miles, who is not a member of the denomination, said he wants Trump to apply diplomatic pressure on Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and urge an end to the inquiry.

"What I would like to see, first of all, is some pressure applied, whether that be through diplomatic channels or through the president himself," Miles told Fox News Digital.

Miles said he remains hopeful the administration will take action and warned that the controversy could establish a troubling precedent for American churches, pointing to past disputes involving religious organizations and government restrictions in the United States.

"They're making this about trying to really smear the church because of specific doctrines that they might hold to, and I think this is a canary in the coal mine for religious liberty across the globe that when we see a Western nation like Australia," Miles said. "The government [is] against the church and against the Christian church in particular, I think this is reason for the rest of the world to wake up."

item.title: Dementia risk may be linked to seemingly harmless daily habit, new research suggests
item.description: Even naps under 30 minutes raised dementia risk 40% in a Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health study of nearly 1,000 older adults.
item.content:encoded:
Frequent daytime napping among older adults has been linked to a higher risk of developing dementia, according to a study published in The Journal of Gerontology: Medical Sciences.

Researchers from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health tracked nearly 1,000 adults age 65 and older who showed no signs of memory or thinking problems when the study began in 2013.

A decade later, the researchers found that daily rest habits — like how often people nap, how long they sleep and whether they fall asleep by accident — are linked to long-term brain health.

ONE TYPE OF SLEEP LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DEMENTIA, PARKINSON'S AND 81 OTHER DISEASES

The study found that participants who napped frequently, defined as most days or every day, had a 48% higher risk of developing dementia compared to those who rarely or never napped.

IMAGE

Whether the naps were intentional also appeared to play a role. Seniors who fell asleep unintentionally had a 39% higher risk, while shorter naps were also linked to poorer outcomes.

Napping for 30 minutes or less was linked to a 40% increased risk of dementia, even after researchers adjusted for other health factors. For naps longer than 30 minutes, the association was less pronounced after researchers accounted for nighttime sleep patterns.

The research team stressed that looking at daytime napping habits gives a much clearer picture of overall health than looking at nighttime sleep alone.

THIS ONE QUESTION MAY REVEAL WHETHER YOUR BODY IS GETTING THE REST IT NEEDS, STUDY FINDS

"Our study highlights the importance of looking beyond just how long people nap and considering other napping characteristics, such as how frequently they nap and whether their naps are intentional," study authors Adam Spira, Ph.D., a professor at the Bloomberg School, and postdoctoral fellow Kening Jiang, Ph.D., told Fox News Digital.

CALLOUT:

"This study provides important longitudinal evidence that frequent and unintentional daytime napping were associated with a higher risk of developing dementia among older adults."

The findings held true even after accounting for nighttime sleep length, daytime drowsiness and indicators of sleep apnea.

"Nighttime sleep and daytime napping are closely related," Spira and Jiang went on. "Daytime napping may compensate for poor nighttime sleep, but it may also reduce the drive to sleep at night, potentially contributing to nighttime sleep disturbances, another important potential risk factor for dementia."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Researchers pointed out that daytime resting does not necessarily cause brain changes. Rather, changing nap habits could be an early warning sign of underlying changes in the brain.

Brain regions that help regulate wakefulness can start to break down in the early stages of dementia, leading to more frequent daytime fatigue, they noted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

To double-check this, the team re-analyzed the data after removing anyone who developed dementia during the first five years.

The link between frequent, accidental naps and dementia remained just as strong, suggesting that changes in napping habits can show up years before a formal diagnosis.

The researchers emphasized that this was an observational study with limitations.

"We did not directly intervene on participants’ napping behaviors to examine whether changing these behaviors would affect their dementia risk," Spira and Jiang told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Although we don’t know whether napping causes dementia, our study findings suggest that daytime napping patterns may be useful indicators of future dementia risk," they added.

The findings suggest that daytime napping patterns in older adults may be worth monitoring, particularly when naps become frequent or happen unintentionally, according to the researchers.

item.title: Data broker opt-out: How retirees can protect their data
item.description: A Minnesota murder suspect's notebook listed 11 people search websites, raising urgent questions about data broker opt-out and online privacy risks.

Your home address, phone number and relatives' names may be sitting on people search websites you've never visited. Anyone who finds those listings could learn more about you than you're comfortable sharing. A data broker opt-out can help reduce that exposure, especially during retirement, when protecting your finances, family and home becomes a priority.

And a tragic case in Minnesota shows why publicly available personal information deserves a closer look. Here's what happened in Minnesota and the steps you can take to make your personal information harder to find online.

WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME

In June 2025, Minnesota lawmaker Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark, were murdered in a targeted attack. State Sen. John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, were seriously injured in a separate shooting. Investigators discovered notebooks containing the names of public officials and a handwritten list of 11 people search websites in the suspect's vehicle. 

The list included TruePeopleSearch, Spokeo, Pipl, PeopleFinders, BeenVerified, Whitepages, TruthFinder, Intelius, Ownerly, USSearch and PeopleLooker. The notes described which services were free and what information someone could find through them.

However, the discovery alone did not establish whether the websites supplied the victims' addresses. On June 11, Vance Boelter pleaded guilty to federal charges in the murders, shootings and stalking of the victims. He was sentenced July 23 to two consecutive life terms, plus 40 years, in federal prison. Separate state charges remain pending. The case raised an unsettling question: How easily could someone find your home address and information about your family?

Data brokers collect information from public records, online activity, commercial databases and other sources. They then combine those details into profiles that businesses and individuals may be able to purchase or access. Some companies specialize in marketing information. Others operate people search websites that make personal details available through free searches or paid reports.

Not every broker collects or sells all this information. Credit reporting agencies also operate under different legal requirements than many people search services. Still, these records can reveal details you never intended to share with strangers. Scammers can use publicly available details to make their stories more convincing. As a result, a suspicious call or message may sound surprisingly personal.

Even if you've never experienced one of these problems, reducing the amount of personal information available online can make it harder for someone to research you.

THE SECRET LIST THAT TELLS SCAMMERS YOU'RE AN EASY TARGET

You can request removal from many people search websites for free. However, each company may have different requirements, and removing a listing doesn't always prevent it from returning.

Here's how to get started.

If you live in California, you now have another option. The state's free Delete Request and Opt-out Platform (DROP) at privacy.ca.gov/drop/ launched in January 2026. It allows eligible residents to submit one deletion request to more than 600 registered data brokers. Beginning August 1, 2026, covered data brokers were required to start processing those requests. 

The system also requires recurring checks for matching information, although legal exceptions apply and removal is not immediate. Other states have their own privacy laws and removal rights, so your options may depend on where you live.

If manually contacting dozens of websites sounds exhausting, a data removal service can handle much of the work for you. You'll typically need to authorize the service to submit removal requests on your behalf. Some providers also offer family plans that cover multiple household members.

Before subscribing, compare the websites each service covers, its removal process, ongoing monitoring features and subscription costs.

Even with automated removal, some personal information may remain publicly accessible. Property ownership records, government databases and certain court records can continue displaying details about you. Data removal services generally cannot force government agencies to delete legally available public records.

Additionally, not every website must honor a removal request. Some services offer custom removals, but legal restrictions and technical limitations can prevent certain information from being deleted.

Removing data broker listings also cannot undo previous data breaches or guarantee that scammers will stop contacting you.

Still, reducing the number of websites exposing your information can make it harder for strangers to find personal details. For retirees, that added privacy can help reduce exposure to targeted scams and unwanted contact.

What concerns me most is how much someone can learn about you without ever meeting you. Your address, family connections and personal history can give scammers information they can use to gain your trust. And once that information starts circulating, controlling where it goes becomes difficult. 

That's why I recommend taking a proactive approach. Start by finding out what's publicly available, remove what you can and keep checking. If the process becomes overwhelming, a reputable data removal service can help with the ongoing work. You may never erase every trace of yourself from the internet, but you can make your personal information harder to find.

item.title: Federal authorities charge 15 in massive $1.8B Southern California medical fraud sweep
item.description: Federal raids across Southern California targeted 15 suspects, including a cardiothoracic surgeon, in nearly $2 billion in healthcare fraud schemes.
item.content:encoded:
Federal authorities conducted predawn raids across Southern California on Thursday, busting suspected fraudsters, including a cardiothoracic surgeon, accused of stealing nearly $2 billion through sham substance abuse programs, unnecessary surgeries and phony hospice care.

In total, 15 people, including six medical professionals, were charged over $1. 8 billion in fraudulent claims submitted to government and private health insurance programs, the Justice Department said.

"These charges include the largest sober home fraud scheme the Department has ever prosecuted and a scheme involving unnecessary invasive procedures that was detected through data analytics," said Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. 

FBI ADDS 2 FUGITIVES TO 'MOST WANTED FRAUDSTERS' LIST AMID HISTORIC $6.5B HEALTHCARE TAKEDOWN: PATEL

"Our message is simple: if you steal health care dollars from the American taxpayer or abuse your position to harm patients, we are coming for you — and the data will lead us to you."

Among the defendants are Dr. Harold Tabaie, 78, of Anaheim, a cardiothoracic surgeon, and his business partner, Hany Malek, 61, a Tarzana chiropractor.

Both are charged in an alleged $135 million scheme to bill Medicare for medically unnecessary atherectomies, invasive arterial procedures using a bladed catheter to clear plaque.

Prosecutors allege Malek posed as a medical doctor to diagnose patients with arterial disease and recommend atherectomies, even though the patients did not have the condition.

CALIFORNIA DOCTOR CONVICTED OF $45M MEDICARE FRAUD SCHEME THAT FUNDED LUXURY VACATIONS AND A $12K CROSSBOW

Tabaie then performed the procedures, sometimes repeatedly on patients for whom previous operations had already failed, according to officials. Authorities noted that several patients suffered extreme pain and discomfort as a result.

Malek also faces charges for allegedly submitting fraudulent Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan applications in 2021. He allegedly fabricated a 25% revenue loss for his business to secure loan funds, which he then spent on personal expenses, family credit cards, other ventures and rare coins.

TOP FEDERAL PROSECUTOR CALLS CALIFORNIA A 'FRAUDSTER'S PARADISE,' WARNS STATE OFFICIALS COULD FACE CHARGES

In a separate case, Nathan Young, 39, and his father, David Young, 71, were charged with operating a $1.6 billion substance abuse scam.

Authorities allege the father-son duo trafficked drug addicts from across the nation to dozens of Los Angeles rehab centers. Federal prosecutors said the vulnerable patients were recruited by "body brokers" Honey Phipps, 42, and Cody Phipps, 36, both of Greenville, Texas.

Body brokerage is the illegal practice of receiving kickbacks to refer insured individuals to specific rehab facilities. Once patients arrived, no actual treatment was provided.

Instead, the Youngs allegedly recycled patients through their facilities to continuously bill insurance companies, even ordering staff to drug patients with sedatives to "knock them out" if they attempted to leave.

VANCE ANTI-FRAUD TASK FORCE SUSPENDS 447 HOSPICES IN LOS ANGELES OVER MORE THAN $600M IN SUSPECTED FRAUD

The duo also allegedly offered drugs to patients, cut them off from communication with family members, prevented them from accessing their belongings and physically blocked them from leaving the facilities to continue billing their insurance policies.

When Nathen Young was informed that a patient wanted to leave detox so he could smoke marijuana, Young instructed that the patient should be given what he wanted, off-site from the detox, to keep him there, prosecutors said.

"It is especially egregious when doctors and other health care professionals, who pledged to do no harm, resort to petty greed and criminality," said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. "Every dollar drained out of our private and public health insurance systems is one less dollar available to those who truly need it."

The sweep also targeted several other major healthcare fraud schemes across the region. In one instance, defendants were charged with stealing more than $140 million by falsely certifying non-terminally ill patients for hospice care.

In a separate prescription fraud scheme, Christina Mareik, 61, of Whittier, was charged for her role in allegedly submitting thousands of bogus prescriptions for high-reimbursement generic drugs to Medi-Cal, California's Medicaid program.

FOUR CHARGED IN ALLEGED BILLION DOLLAR HEALTHCARE FRAUD TIED TO RUSSIAN TRANSNATIONAL CRIMINAL ORGANIZATION

Additionally, Dr. Hassan Badday, 48, of Los Angeles, and Dr. Robby Ayoub, 52, of Huntington Beach, were charged with taking illegal kickbacks from a Houston laboratory marketer in exchange for ordering unnecessary Medicare genetic tests.

item.title: Accused Philadelphia cop killer Eric Lewis faces new federal gun, robbery charges after deadly ambush

item.content:encoded:
The man accused of ambushing two Philadelphia police officers, killing one and wounding another, now faces federal charges.

Eric Lewis, 35, is accused of fatally shooting Philadelphia Police Officer Shane Seiber and wounding his partner. He faces a range of state charges, among them murder, homicide of a law enforcement officer, attempted murder, 10 counts of attempted homicide of a law enforcement officer, aggravated assault, terroristic threats and other related offenses.

In addition to the state-level charges, Lewis on Thursday was indicted on federal charges of interstate commerce by robbery, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, possession of a firearm and ammunition by a felon, theft of a firearm that has moved in interstate commerce, and possession of a stolen firearm and stolen ammunition.

At a news conference on Thursday, David Metcalf, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, said that Lewis wasn't allowed to carry a gun under U.S. law.

"Under federal law, Eric Lewis is not allowed to possess a firearm. He is a convicted felon under federal law. He is certainly not allowed to steal a firearm, and under federal law, he is certainly prohibited from using any firearm to rob, shoot, and kill a police officer, as a result of those actions," Metcalf said.

"No one attacks law enforcement without facing the consequences," he said when the new federal charges were announced.

SUSPECT IN DEADLY PHILADELPHIA POLICE AMBUSH FACES 76 CHARGES, ORDERED HELD WITHOUT BAIL

The wounded officer, Hector Rodriguez III, who remains hospitalized but in stable condition, was shot 12 times. A short time later, both officers were discovered wounded on the porch.

Seiber, 40, was an Air Force veteran and father of two who spent 10 years serving with the Philadelphia Police Department. He leaves behind his wife, a 7-year-old son and a 3-year-old daughter.

Court records show that Lewis, an employee of the Philadelphia Water Department, has a criminal history that dates back to 2012.

A 2012 conviction for theft and receiving stolen property marked the start of Lewis' criminal record. The following year, he was convicted of gun-related offenses and simple assault, for which he received probation.

In 2018, Lewis entered a guilty plea to disorderly conduct involving fighting and was again sentenced to probation.

Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner earlier in October said that Lewis was acquitted in a previous murder case, blaming police misconduct for the outcome.

"Why this man was out of custody? The answer is this, this man is out of custody because a balanced, good and fair judge did what he had to do because two absolutely excellent prosecutors did everything humanly possible with a case and an investigation that was so deeply flawed. It was not just full of errors and mistakes, very serious ones, But some of the conduct involving one police officer... And one detective is arguably criminal. Yes, I said criminal," Krasner said.

GOT A TIP?

Krasner said the police officer, who was in a relationship with the defendant's sister, attempted to "torpedo" his testimony "by making up a complete lie."

In a statement to Fox News, the Philadelphia Police Department said, "Assigning blame while families are grieving does nothing to advance accountability or support those affected."

"True leadership does not seek to assign fault in a moment like this. It stands with the families. And when the time comes, it holds itself to the same scrutiny it asks of others," the police department said.
